value.title: Check-ins and photo locations: a draft "place pin" record + a new Eurosky place service
value.description: Hi y’all, I’m writing this with 2 hats on. Hat 1, app dev: I make https://www.flashes.blue and https://www.skeetsapp.com . Both are about to ship locations: Flashes will let people say where their photos and videos were taken, Skeets will get check-ins. Hat 2, Eurosky: to power that, we’ve just started places.eurosky.tech , a place service for the open social web. Behind the URL: a worldwide gazetteer rebuilt monthly from Overture (places, divisions, addresses), Foursquare Open Source Places and OpenStreetMap; records merged across the sources (~112M places), ranked with Wikipedia importance. It offers: suggestions for a position: nearby places, the street, and the areas that contain it (district, city, country), for e.g. a check-in picker; type-ahead search; a privacy-preserving fixed ~1 km squares query API: cacheable, and the server only learns which square you asked for. It’s built on ATGeo’s conventions: every place carries its ATGeo URN in origin (plus sameAs for the same place in other sources), areas are Overture divisions as in garganorn, and the squares follow garganorn’s idea that a client fetches a whole area so the server never learns its position. It also answers org.atgeo.getPlace , so ATGeo clients can look places up by URN (for example McDonald’s at Hermannplatz ); the tile interface ( getTiles ) could follow if ATGeo apps want a European server. The code is public: https://github.com/eurosky-social/eurosky-places Before my apps ship, I’d like to agree the record format with you rather than add yet another one. This picks up the check-in thread from last summer , this time with something concrete. Here’s the draft: https://github.com/eurosky-social/eurosky-places/blob/main/docs/place-pin.md (lexicon: pin.json ) The short version: A small record next to the post, one place per record. It can be limited to some of the post’s photos or videos, named by their blob CIDs, so it works for any media in any app. Without a post it’s a check-in on its own. It follows where we landed in 2025: no at:// URIs for external places. The record carries the place’s ATGeo URN in origin , plus the subset readers need: name, a coarse category, a point, the containing areas and the place’s IDs in other sources. It uses the same field names as org.atgeo.place , and community.lexicon.location.* objects for locations. About 0.5–1.3 KB per record. The author picks the level: venue, street, district, city, region or country. Coordinates are rounded to it, and the device’s own position is never written. Readers can group by origin (and sameAs ), draw maps and show thumbnails without any gazetteer lookup or fetching the post. Constellation could answer “all pins at this place”. It’s under our namespace ( social.eurosky.place.pin ) for now but I’d rather see it become org.atgeo.checkin or a lexicon.community record if that’s the better home. Questions I’d love input on: Home: org.atgeo.checkin , lexicon.community, or leave it with us? The dataset name for Fours

Hi y’all, I’m writing this with 2 hats on.

 Hat 1, app dev: I make https://www.flashes.blue and https://www.skeetsapp.com . Both are about to ship locations: Flashes will let people say where their photos and videos were taken, Skeets will get check-ins.

 Hat 2, Eurosky: to power that, we’ve just started places.eurosky.tech , a place service for the open social web. Behind the URL:

 a worldwide gazetteer rebuilt monthly from Overture (places, divisions, addresses), Foursquare Open Source Places and OpenStreetMap;

 records merged across the sources (~112M places), ranked with Wikipedia importance.

 It offers:

 suggestions for a position: nearby places, the street, and the areas that contain it (district, city, country), for e.g. a check-in picker;

 type-ahead search; 

 a privacy-preserving fixed ~1 km squares query API: cacheable, and the server only learns which square you asked for.

 It’s built on ATGeo’s conventions: every place carries its ATGeo URN in origin (plus sameAs for the same place in other sources), areas are Overture divisions as in garganorn, and the squares follow garganorn’s idea that a client fetches a whole area so the server never learns its position. It also answers org.atgeo.getPlace , so ATGeo clients can look places up by URN (for example McDonald’s at Hermannplatz ); the tile interface ( getTiles ) could follow if ATGeo apps want a European server. The code is public: https://github.com/eurosky-social/eurosky-places 

 Before my apps ship, I’d like to agree the record format with you rather than add yet another one. This picks up the check-in thread from last summer , this time with something concrete.

 Here’s the draft: https://github.com/eurosky-social/eurosky-places/blob/main/docs/place-pin.md (lexicon: pin.json )

 The short version:

 A small record next to the post, one place per record. It can be limited to some of the post’s photos or videos, named by their blob CIDs, so it works for any media in any app. Without a post it’s a check-in on its own.

 It follows where we landed in 2025: no at:// URIs for external places. The record carries the place’s ATGeo URN in origin , plus the subset readers need: name, a coarse category, a point, the containing areas and the place’s IDs in other sources. It uses the same field names as org.atgeo.place , and community.lexicon.location.* objects for locations. About 0.5–1.3 KB per record.

 The author picks the level: venue, street, district, city, region or country. Coordinates are rounded to it, and the device’s own position is never written.

 Readers can group by origin (and sameAs ), draw maps and show thumbnails without any gazetteer lookup or fetching the post. Constellation could answer “all pins at this place”.

 It’s under our namespace ( social.eurosky.place.pin ) for now but I’d rather see it become org.atgeo.checkin or a lexicon.community record if that’s the better home.

 Questions I’d love input on:

 Home: org.atgeo.checkin , lexicon.community, or leave it with us?

 The dataset name for Foursquare in URNs (we currently use foursquare.com ).

 A shared coarse category list, or app-defined?

 Is a pin without a post the check-in record, or should a check-in be its own record with text?

 Some things we learned building the service that may help garganorn:

 Foursquare Open Source Places isn’t discontinued. It has been gated on Hugging Face since October 2025, and works with a token once you accept the terms.

 Only ~38% of Overture place IDs survived a year (Overture re-matched its places in July 2026), against ~99% of Foursquare IDs over 19 months and ~97% of OSM IDs over 5 months. That’s why the draft puts the longest-lived ID in origin .

 Overture’s September 2026 release added company-registry records (BrightQuery) that aren’t venues. Also, Overture’s own “signals” source shouldn’t count as a second confirmation.

 Overture piles up records at a city’s reference point when it only knows the town: 428 at one point in Nairobi, including national parks.
Very cool! I’m curious how this compares to beaconbits.app by @montoulieu.dev

Hi Sebastian, thanks for sharing this. I’m fairly new to the lexicon side of things, so please correct me where I get it wrong.

 It’s a nice coincidence. I just released my app, Placita , in private alpha. One of my goals now is to look at the wider Atmosphere and see how I can connect with what others are building. Your post came at the right moment. I would be happy to help where I can, because getting a few of these formats to line up is exactly what I hope for.

 Placita is a saved-places app. People keep places they want to visit or have been to, with tags, notes and a rating. It is not a check-in app, and I will leave check-ins to others for now. I use OpenStreetMap today and have not worked with Foursquare data, so your notes on it were useful.

 My approach is to use open data where I can and add richer sources where they help. I also want to build from the bottom up. People start with their own places in their own account, and the data gets richer over time. For that to work across apps, records need a shared way to point at the same place. That is why your URNs interest me. I am happy to add optional fields to my lexicon so our records line up.

 On your questions:

 Home (your question 1): I prefer a neutral one, ATGeo or lexicon.community. It is better long term, because several check-in lexicons already exist.

 Categories (your question 3): a shared coarse list sounds useful. Placita has a longer list of its own, and I could map it onto yours. I would keep it open for new values.

 One more question, from testing in Barcelona, where I live. I took 53 Foursquare places around Gràcia, El Born and Eixample that your suggestions endpoint matches to an OSM place. For 45 of them, getPlace on the OSM record points back to the Foursquare ID. For 8 it does not. One example is Cactus Bar in El Born. The suggestions answer says the Foursquare place and OSM node 4321293689 are the same, but getPlace on that node has an empty sameAs . An app that only knows the OSM ID, like mine, would not find the Foursquare pin in those cases. Is this a known gap, or do the links only show up in some answers?

 @montoulieu.dev , I would be interested in your view too, since Beacon Bits already has a check-in record.

Hi Sebastian, this lands nicelyon something I’m working on. CultureBlocs (intro here: https://discourse.atmosphere.community/t/cultureblocs-data-points-on-cultural-and-creative-activity/1321 ) records cultural activity: venues publish their profile and listings, and people mint “I went” records against events. Places are the missing join.

 A few thoughts from the cultural-venue side:

 Home: +1 for a neutral home (ATGeo or Lexicon Community).

 Reusable place reference: could the place reference itself (URN in origin, sameAs, name, level, areas) be a reusable def as well as part of the pin record? I’d like to embed it in our own records (a visit or screening, a venue profile, an event location) rather than write a separate pin alongside each one. Your precision levels and the never-write-device-position rule fit our privacy defaults exactly.

 Categories: a shared coarse list, open-ended, with gallery, museum, cinema, theatre, music venue, festival site and library in it.

 Venue edge cases: venues nest (a hall, cinemas and a gallery in one building), some are temporary (art fair tents, festival stages) and won’t be in any gazetteer, and they rename and move. How would you handle a place that isn’t in the gazetteer yet?

 Happy to test against places.eurosky.tech with some London venues.

 mark

I’m drafting this: Atmospheric Workspace OS 

 In summary, I love what @scottlanoue.com is cooking up with the Atmosphere OS . The road to an actual OS however is very long, and I think one way to arrive at something tangible sooner rather than later is a Rambox -like omniclient for atmospheric apps, aka an atmospheric apps launcher .

 Skjermbilde 2026-10-25 140226 1810×733 207 KB 

 Most apps on the atmosphere don’t have the bandwidth to maintain a desktop distribution, even though many of these apps are useful in a workplace context, a few of which are even offline-first, like Reams by @hyl.st 

 What if we pooled our efforts to make one canonical Atmospheric Launcher app for the desktop (Windows, Mac, Linux)? Perhaps even starting web-first and going desktop from there; see the approach suggested by @disnetdev.com below.

 There are different ways to go about this. The experience I’m reaching for is a downloadable desktop app that:

 Only asks me to log into my atmosphere account(s) once, and then keeps me logged in, ideally with even greater persistence than the average browser experience (atmo apps have a tendency towards very short auth sessions).

 facilitates local backups & key rotations

 built-in widget for atproto calls 

 unified notifications

 ???

 Option 1: Tauri omniclient

 Ferdium is a long-standing open source alternative to the likes of Rambox, which could be forked into an atmo launcher. I started exploring this with a Tauri fork of Ferdium called Ferx .

 It’s pretty neat to see how easy it is to add additional apps to the client:

 Skjermbilde 2026-10-27 093005 1204×1078 66.6 KB 

 Skjermbilde 2026-10-27 093034 1918×1078 227 KB 

 However, logins don’t work right. Ferx doesn’t have a built-in password storage and it also seems to run every app in a separate session, so even though I’ve already logged into one of these apps (Skyreader) with my atmo account, the rest don’t even know I already logged into my atmo account, which is a step down from the regular browser experience.

 Option 2: Chrome derivative

 This is the least proven option so far, but it’s how many of the Rambox-likes work, by simply sprinkling a thin additional layer on top of stock Chrome. This would be the same approach as the ideal long-term case that is Beaver , except the purpose of an atmospheric Chrome derivative would be an expedient time-to-market.

 I’ve no idea how feasible it is to “simply layer some atmospheric stuff on top of Chrome”, but I keep being told we’re supposed to think more ambitiously in this brave new age of auto-coding. I’ve got my qualms about that but perhaps in this case that line of thinking is appropriate.

 Option 3: Web-first launcher

 @disnetdev.com came up with another approach

 so this is really interesting and got me thinking if you could do an atmospheric workspace of cooperating apps without needing a desktop app. a few tokens later…

 https://atworkplace-shell.strand-source.workers.dev/ 

 GitHub - disnet/atlauncher · GitHub 

 requires apps to opt-in to framing and then follow a small protocol: atlauncher/docs/PROTOCOL.md at main · disnet/atlauncher · GitHub 

 by framing and being atproto aware lets you do cool things like real unread badges without scraping titles and at:// link handling that route to the appropriate app.

 I’ve been chatting with @scottlanoue.com @hyl.st and @disnetdev.com about this and this is where we’re at so far.

FOSDEM 2027: AT Protocol Devroom

 What is FOSDEM

 FOSDEM is an annual two-day, free admission, fully volunteer-run conference bringing together developers to meet, share ideas and collaborate on topics in the free open source software space. The event takes place in Brussels, Belgium on January 30-31, 2027.

 About the AT Protocol devroom

 AT Protocol, also nicknamed Atproto, is a protocol which allows the creation of new social experiments by providing a modular system around identity, data and interoperability. Originally developed by Bluesky PBC for its microblogging app, it now serves millions of users through a network of applications and services called the Atmosphere, and is continuously evolving and growing with new capabilities and upgrades ranging from large-scale data replay to private community spaces and shared formats across apps.

 The AT Protocol devroom is dedicated to talks around the apps built on the protocol, infrastructure and development of the protocol itself, as well as the community shaping the Atmosphere, and beyond. We encourage people to apply regardless of their background, gender, or how much speaking experience they have, and aim to curate an agenda with varying perspectives and backgrounds.

 Suggested topics

 Applications: what cool application did you build?

 Data that isn’t public by default: private records, group-scoped and shared data, and what changes for an application when not everything is on the firehose.

 Running the infrastructure: self-hosting a PDS, relays, AppViews, feed generators, labelers. What are your stories?

 Protocol: new features like permissioned spaces.

 Development: independent implementations of protocol components, SDKs, and libraries in different programming languages.

 Moderation: what is your opinion or usage of the stackable moderation and labeling systems?

 Account portability and data ownership: what actually works today and what is still missing.

 Interoperability and bridges: atproto and ActivityPub and other open social protocols.

 Governance: specification processes, and the path toward an ecosystem with multiple independent stewards.

 Research, measurement, and analysis of the network.

 Critical perspectives: where atproto’s design falls short and what should change.

 And more! Please don’t hesitate to suggest a talk that relates to AT Protocol even beyond the suggested topics.

 We welcome talks from protocol implementers, application developers, infrastructure operators, researchers, and community members. Talks from people who are skeptical of the design are as welcome as talks from people building on it. Demos and lessons-learned talks are strongly encouraged over roadmap presentations.

 Submitting a talk

 We offer two talk lengths:

 Standard slots are 25 minutes, including time for Q&A.

 Lightning talk slots are 13 minutes, including time for Q&A.

 Because of the large number of new apps developed every month using the protocol, we recommend the lightning slots for talks and presentations on projects you’ve developed, and the longer standard slot for deeper takes on the protocol, its infrastructure, development and surrounding community.

 We prioritise talks that have not been previously held or submitted to other conferences, and aim to produce a diverse spread of perspectives. We encourage both first-time speakers and AT Protocol veterans to submit talks.

 Important dates

 Date 
 Milestone 

 November 20, 23:59 EET 
 CfP closes 

 December 4 
 Speakers notified 

 December 7 
 Devroom schedule published 

 How to submit a talk

 Go to FOSDEM pretalx .

 Select “AT Protocol” from the Track dropdown menu.

 In the submission notes, tell us which talk length you’re interested in (25 minutes or 13 minutes).

 Make sure to submit your proposal by November 20, 23:59 EET .

 Code of Conduct

 We expect all speakers and attendees to follow the FOSDEM Code of Conduct in all parts of the devroom, from talks, questions and discussions to every other interaction.

 Contact us

 You can reach AT protocol devroom managers Viivi Marttinen and Édouard Paris at at-protocol-devroom-manager@fosdem.org in all questions related to the devroom, including volunteering in the room.

 See you at the AT Protocol devroom!

value.title: [Atp] Re: Floats support summary
value.description: Hi Volker, Thank you for picking this back up. I continue to have strong concerns about depending on JSON numeric encoding alone to determine whether a number is intended to be an integer or float. The JSON data model is clear in having only a single overall numeric type, and I think we need a more general and robust solution to this modeling problem than relying on observed implementation behaviors. In many situations and use-cases the encoding and distinction is not important, but because atproto is content-addressed, it is important. I think a wrapper encoding like the ‘$float’ option you mention would be more suitable. In your analysis of implementation behaviors, you noted JavaScript and Go as language ecosystems where special care and configuration is required to ensure consistent encoding behavior. Those are both popular languages in general, and top languages in the atproto ecosystem today. As noted above I don’t think the behaviors of individual JSON implementations are particularly important for making this decision, but it is concerning to me that these languages would not work reliably “out of the box”. I’m putting together some more specific examples and a counter-proposal to share with the list. I’d love to get feedback on all this from more folks, both atproto developers and IETF community folks. The upcoming IETF 127 meeting seems like a good time frame for converging on a path forward. –bryan

value.title: Floats on ATProto
value.description: I’ve spent quite some time on how floats could be added to the ATProto data model. Here’s the full write up: Floats on ATProto | vmx - the blllog. Feel free to discuss it here or reply to my Bluesky post at @vmx.cx on Bluesky .
value.textContent:
I’ve spent quite some time on how floats could be added to the ATProto data model. Here’s the full write up: Floats on ATProto | vmx - the blllog. 

 Feel free to discuss it here or reply to my Bluesky post at @vmx.cx on Bluesky .

Hey! Thanks for the proposal. I appreciate the effort that went into this, and it’s clearly well thought through.

 If my understanding is right, round-tripping requires either being schema-aware or using a custom JSON parser (for identifying “.” in numbers). I’m not saying those are unworkable, but they are a bit unfortunate. We’ll need to think through the impact/implications.

 A couple meta points on process:

 We really don’t have a lot of throughput on protocol stuff at the moment with permissioned data in the works and prepping for the first IETF working group meeting. This is subtle enough & has a wide enough impact that I don’t think we’ll be able to dedicate the time it needs to get it over the line

 The JSON & CBOR encodings are part of the IETF working group charter! This is actually a great topic of conversation for the mailing list . The fact that this is part of the charter makes me reticent to make a change of this size to the spec outside of the working group

 If just having something for floats is imperative, adding a string format for “float” is much lower lift & less of a spec change. Kinda ugly and probably makes no one happy, but sometimes that’s the sign of a good compromise

dholms.xyz: 

 using a custom JSON parser (for identifying “.” in numbers)

 The nice thing is that you don’t need a custom JSON parser. Usually all parsers do that already.

 dholms.xyz: 

 I don’t think we’ll be able to dedicate the time it needs to get it over the line

 In which time frame. Surely the sooner the better, but there isn’t really much urgency.

 dholms.xyz: 

 The JSON & CBOR encodings are part of the IETF working group charter! This is actually a great topic of conversation for the mailing list .

 I’m happy to start a discussion there. Though I guess it’s again a matter of timing. I don’t want to derail things, I’m sure there are working group things with higher priority.

 dholms.xyz: 

 If just having something for floats is imperative, adding a string format for “float” is much lower lift & less of a spec change. Kinda ugly and probably makes no one happy, but sometimes that’s the sign of a good compromise 

 I thought about that. In terms of “breaking things”, I don’t think it would be more or less harmful, so let’s just do the real thing. I’m happy to spend more time on it. I guess I still haven’t fully grasp the impact on where things could break.

I also want to chime in that it is great to see this all gone through with motivating examples, good write-ups, and working code.

 I’m pretty interested in this, but want to verify a few things with experiments. In particular, which popular languages reliably read and write integers and floats differently from JSON? And maybe also produce some test vectors and worked example code to demonstrate corner-cases.

 I’m overall pretty hesitant to rely on JSON text encoding including ‘.0’ or not to distinguish integers from floats throughout the numerical range. At the end of the day the JSON data model only has a single numerical type (the core issue here), and relying on common behaviors doesn’t feel very robust.

 I think it is actually relatively common for atproto implementations to need to work with un-typed / no-schema data and want to be able to pass it through multiple contexts and have it come back with the same CID. I think you have broad experience with this sort of thing, but just to lay out some of my thinking, you might want to persist record data in PostgreSQL as JSONB type (supporting rich queries), read it back later, and be able to confirm the CID version. You might get record data back from an HTTP API in JSON format, with a CID along side it, and want to be able to confirm the CID matches the data. The ‘unknown’ Lexicon type allows stuffing arbitrary bytes in.

 What i’d be kind of thinking of is to have an unambiguous JSON encoding, and then CBOR can use the obvious/efficient typed encoding. The JSON encoding could look like the existing CID link and bytes special objects:

 {
 "$float": 123.456
}

 (the float value itself could also be in string format, or even base64 or hex encoded)

 This isn’t super fun/aesthetic in raw JSON, but for the subset of application code which is schema-aware, this could all be transparently handled, the same way bytestrings or CID links are today. Though maybe a “float” string format in Lexicon would also work this way (get converted to/from floats via codegen).

 In addition to the “is it a float or an integer” ambiguity, we’d need to settle on how special float values are handled, and get that tested and rolled out to the entire ecosystem. I think IPLD DAG-CBOR didn’t get too far in the weeds on this, but I’ve seen a couple different deterministic CBOR flavors floating around the IETF with different rules about this (eg, are NaN and +Inf/-Inf allowed, with both signs or not, etc). There is work happening there, and it should probably be possible to settle on a spec, but I think research/consensus would be needed. I personally have lingering anxiety knowing how complex hardware support for IEEE floats is, and would want to do some more research and experimentation that things like FPU rounding mode wouldn’t come in to play. It would really suck if atproto didn’t work reliably or in an interoperable way on obscure CPU instruction sets or old computers or something like that. This might just be FUD, but I’ve been bitten by softfloat, weird libc/newlib ports, things like that.

Thanks again @vmx.cx for the proposal! Chiming in here as well to say that it would be great to see this, although I understand that there’s a long backlog of protocol-related things that need to happen first.

 For a couple of months now (except for when my code crashes ) I’ve been posting astronomical transients from the NASA GCN onto the protocol, in a machine-readable form that science cases could hook into. This alert stream is really just a small test - in principle, astronomy has hundreds of thousands of daily alerts that we could post - but so far, I’m seeing low latency and ease of use that would make using atproto for data streaming very attractive to us in astronomy. Transients aren’t my main area of research, but I’ve reached out to a few people who do it full-time and want to collaborate on integrating atproto into more of our workflows.

 The catch is that most of our data is floating point, such as data on this gravitational wave or this gamma-ray burst . After a lot of trying, the only consistently functional solution that I have right now is to stringify the entire external data, which is quite ugly - but since most fields are floats, or even arrays of floats, coercing an external schema full of floats to work with atproto becomes a massive headache.

 Arrays of floats or mixed type arrays are particularly painful right now on atproto, and deserve a ‘special’ mention. For instance - should you stringify the whole thing? When it contains floats only sometimes, do you stringify always? How can you anticipate that? How can you tell what a stringified float is vs. a string that could be a number but isn’t? It quickly becomes a very big headache, centered around what is probably the most common type of data for us.

 Now, it might then seem a bit like using atproto for streaming scientific data is a stretch, or a niche issue that isn’t worth solving. But I think that it is actually perfect for streaming data, and I could envision a world where all scientific metadata (or if it’s small/time-critical like our transients, the data itself) gets posted to the atproto. It just has too many advantages and beats every single other solution I’m aware of:

 The extremely low overhead to post records as a producer makes it low-effort to adopt & run. This compares to existing solutions (like everyone self-hosting their own kafka stream for every single project) which require much more technical know-how and compute

 Everything being public and a real-time stream is fantastic for data discoverability, be that among ourselves or for involving the public

 The low overhead to subscribe to events as a consumer (e.g. with jetstream) makes it very easy to hook into event streams, and even many at the same time. (It still needs improvement, but nebra distills this into one easy to use Python function.)

 So, motivating post aside, I think that having floats on the protocol somehow would be a very useful goal to be able to capture the scientific ecosystem. atproto is a lot harder to sell for that purpose right now because floats don’t have first-class support, and it’s an awkward part of my sales pitch right now because it just doesn’t make atproto feel like a serious fit for scientific data. I’d be in favour of vmx’s proposal, or at least something - like a dedicated string-float type that is recognizable and could easily be encoded/decoded, maybe even at the PDS level somehow. But honestly, if there’s a way to bake support for floats into the protocol on the most basic level, then it would be fantastic long-term for being able to benefit the scientific ecosystem, and probably many other use cases too.

 (P.S.: I live in Vienna - if it would be useful to have me at IETF or even just to meet at the side to chat & coordinate, then I’d be happy to)

vmx.cx: 

 I’m happy to start a discussion there. Though I guess it’s again a matter of timing. I don’t want to derail things, I’m sure there are working group things with higher priority.

 Not derailing at all! There need to be experts and champions for different things in the protocol. Appreciate the time you’ve put in here.

emily.space: 

 I live in Vienna - if it would be useful to have me at IETF or even just to meet at the side to chat & coordinate, then I’d be happy to

 I won’t be there but I’ve been trying to get someone to organize a community side event. eg pick a time during the week that doesn’t overlap with on-site IETF stuff, run some sessions during the day (floats seems like a great topic), maybe an evening meal.

 @cypherhippie.bsky.social is also in Vienna and maybe has a room at the university that can be used?

I’ve been using scaled integers very successfully for both geo points (though I’d prefer to be using a “real"“ geo lexicon) and for recording sensor data. See “info” here , and the “observation” section in particular. This is a similar method to how protobuf stores floats, and avoids the “stringification” issue, which I looked at but dismissed as too messy and error-prone. So far, it’s worked very well.

I’ve worked with GeoJSON before and true floats are definitely a bit of a footgun there.

(They give you vastly more precision than needed, so without a custom serialiser it’s way too easy to blow up the file size with decimal digits for real-world administrative data.)

 I think that the appropriate scaling factor is too app-specific to set in stone in a generic geo lexicon though, since it’s always a tradeoff with file size. A location scrobbler probably doesn’t need sub-metre precision, while for a geocaching app that can be appropriate and for mapping building outlines it’s basically a requirement.

Fixed integer scale factors will work in some cases, but it becomes inefficient if you have a very big or small number. I guess an on-protocol float format that can do varying scale factors could have an integer part in for the number and a scale factor, all defined in an object.

 I would still rather have first-class floating point number support as this could get annoying to parse if you have many in one record, though it would work on-protocol right now. E.g., 7.536×10^(-55) could be:

 {
 $type: "community.lexicon.float",
 num: 7536,
 scale: -58
}

I’m a bit skeptical of scaled or fractional integers. They are a different numerical model from IEEE floats, which I think is what most folks would be expecting here. They are popular in some fields (eg, representing monetary values), but those are usually distinct, and can be represented as simple integer arrays.

 I’m curious to hear from proponents whether the { “$float”: 1.05 } JSON encoding would be acceptable. If the goal is to have the JSON representation of record data match things like GeoJSON, it isn’t going to be one-to-one, a translation will be needed. But if the goal is to map in to programming language representations (structs, dataclasses, records, whatever), with SDKs handling the conversion, I think it works fine.

 I think the string “format” option should also still be considered. That would not impact the data model or encodings at all, and be far less disruptive to implement.

 Another place that data types are represented is query params in XRPC API endpoints. These basically get passed around as strings before being parsed in a lexicon-aware way, so I think the concerns for adding a float type there are simpler.

 If we decide to go ahead, we’d probably want to coordinate with the DRISL folks. The current DRISL spec mentions floats a bit, though recommends minimizing their usage aggressively. They also say to simply not use NaNs etc. I think we’d need to come up more documentation/norms around what that means: what is an encoding library supposed to do if it encounters a NaN or Inf value when encoding? When decoding? Throw an error and treat the entire record as invalid?

 The Hypha Coop got a grant to carefully implement the DASL/DRISL specification, and that included a test suite and compliance matrix. This includes float support. You can view it here:

 hyphacoop.github.io 

 DASL Testing 

 Having thought on it a bit, I think the best venue for this discussion is probably the IETF working group. We do talk about the data model in the very first IETF document (the “repo” draft text). Making a change to the data model used for records is one of the lowest-level / most-core aspects of the protocol, and will need broad ecosystem and implementation buy-in, which is what the standards process is intended to enable. We are kicking off the working group in Vienna in about a month, and I expect the group to be working on the document this would fall under through the remainder of the year (at least). @emily.space and @vmx.cx , it would be great to have you participate if you are able, eg by emailing the list ahead of time and/or doing a short presentation to the WG introducing the topic. It is pretty easy to participate in the WG meetings remotely: you can apply for an automatic free waiver for the remote registration fee (and this is widely encouraged by IETF leadership). I think you could probably also be eligible for a fee waiver for in-person participation, or we (as an ecosystem) can try to find funding to cover that cost.

 Something related we need to work through is consistent handling of invalid record data encoding. If this isn’t handled consistently through the ecosystem, it can result in both janky/inconsistent experiences, and abuse vectors. For example, if some implementations enforce the data model strictly (rejecting invalid records), but others do not, then some records will “show up” in some places but not others. If the record creates abusive/harassing content, and moderation tools reject the record, but some app clients don’t, it can become a moderation bypass hack. This isn’t specific to floats in the data model, but does motivate taking care and ensuring the data model is defined and implemented consistently.

Thanks @bnewbold.net to put more thought into this.

 bnewbold.net: 

 I’m curious to hear from proponents whether the { “$float”: 1.05 } JSON encoding would be acceptable.

 The biggest issue is if you have array of floats, or even nested ones like in GeoJSON. You could allow something like {”$float”: [[0.1, 0.42], [4.2, 82.1]]} , but then you kind of end up with your own mini-language with additional edge cases.

 I think the easiest/best way is to it with a convention (just as $float would be one), but settle with digits only => integer, else it’s a float. It’s easy to remember and also not that hard to implement, as it often is implemented that way anyway.

 This “it’s already often the case” it not something I make up, but I’m currently testing. It’s almost ready, but it needs a few more cleanups. I’m creating a survey across programming languages how they deal with the convention I mention above. I try hard to make that as useful as possible. My goal is not to make it look good for my position, but to really show where the issues are, so we can make a good informed decision about it.

 There’s more to say about that, but I’ll do that once I’m done and happy with the testing.

 bnewbold.net: 

 I think the string “format” option should also still be considered. That would not impact the data model or encodings at all, and be far less disruptive to implement.

 I’ve thought about that quite a bit. I see the CBOR encoding as the actual data that should be used. The JSON is just a representation of it. What matters is the CBOR and ideally once you have the CBOR, you never try to recreate it again from some other format. If floats are strings in there, you can’t really process them later on, e.g. to query on them. You could parse every string and check if it contains digits, points, and e’s only and then decide that it must be float.

 bnewbold.net: 

 Making a change to the data model used for records is one of the lowest-level / most-core aspects of the protocol, and will need broad ecosystem and implementation buy-in

 When I read over the IETF drafts (I really had only a quick look, I still need to read them closely) I wonder how much the data model actually matters. Isn’t for the repo the encoded CBOR just an opaque blob? Don’t get me wrong, I want to get this standardized hopefully as soon as possible. I’m just unsure how critical it is for the rest of the protocol.

 I’m happy to participate in the IETF process.

 bnewbold.net: 

 They also say to simply not use NaNs etc. I think we’d need to come up more documentation/norms around what that means

 Currently using non-numbers is considered an error on encoding and decoding (which is also what the current DAG-CBOR implementation do). Whether that renders the whole record invalid or not is an open question, but I think it should.

Thanks so much for the reply & thoughts @bnewbold.net !

 bnewbold.net: 

 I’m curious to hear from proponents whether the { “$float”: 1.05 } JSON encoding would be acceptable.

 As with @vmx.cx , I worry that this will quite quickly get quite messy with arrays of floats or mixed type arrays, but it’s at least clear that there’s a floating point number there. I don’t think that would necessarily always be the case with float-strings, because:

 bnewbold.net: 

 I think the string “format” option should also still be considered. That would not impact the data model or encodings at all, and be far less disruptive to implement.

 How would the string formatting be identified? Would ‘float-strings’ have to start with certain characters? This ought to be a convention across the protocol, e.g. with floats denoted something like “f_123.456” . There would be potential for unwanted conversions if a string happens to start with the identifying characters (e.g. like “f_” ). There might be ways to fix this at the level of individual lexicons, such as some convention for which fields are allowed to have float-strings, but I could see it getting quite complicated quite quickly and probably spinning out into many different solutions. For instance, matadisco records sometimes contain additional not-in-the-lexicon metadata; in those cases, there would be no lexicon to follow to know which strings starting with the identifier should or shouldn’t be interpreted as floats, and it could get quite messy.

 bnewbold.net: 

 @emily.space and @vmx.cx , it would be great to have you participate if you are able, eg by emailing the list ahead of time and/or doing a short presentation to the WG introducing the topic.

 This should be possible! I should be able to come in person too, as long as I can get a fee waiver somehow. (it would make more sense than participating remotely from only ~3 km away)

I can send an email to the mailing list, I’ll try to squeeze it in next week.

 I probably can’t make it to the meeting, but @bumblefudge.com will be there in person and can talk about it.

vmx.cx: 

 This “it’s already often the case” it not something I make up, but I’m currently testing. It’s almost ready, but it needs a few more cleanups. I’m creating a survey across programming languages how they deal with the convention I mention above. I try hard to make that as useful as possible. My goal is not to make it look good for my position, but to really show where the issues are, so we can make a good informed decision about it.

 Alright, I’ve finally finished that work, it can be read at JSON, floats and native types | vmx - the blllog. and GitHub - vmx/json-floats-native-types: Survey of how floats and integers are distinguished in various programming languages/databases · GitHub .

 I think it contains quite a few things to unpack. But I want to concentrate on the two most important ones which I hope we find agreement on:

 We don’t need a special syntax for floats, it’s already there. Add a fraction or exponent to your JSON number and it’s a float. Most systems support this already, so it’s less work to do it that way than adding a special way to all of them

 This is maybe the most important one: For preparation we need the ATProto implementations to stop treating a small enough JSON value with an exponent and no fraction as an integer value. I consider this a bug, no other system in the survey does that and I think we shouldn’t be an outlier here.

bnewbold.net: 

 it would be good to mention this topic on the mailing list soon (eg, a couple weeks ahead of the actual meeting).

 For any interested party, here’s the thread on the IETF ATP WG mailing list: [Atp] Float support in data model .

It’s been a while, so it’s time to get this done.

 I’ve sent an email to the IETF ATP Working Group mailing list , wrote a [blog post]( Floats on ATProto summary | vmx - the blllog. ) with a summary and a conclusion and opened a PR on the draft spec .

 It doesn’t mean it will be approved. So please, once more, show your support, ideally on the ATP Working Group mailing list. Though anywhere else is also fine.

value.description: Cross-posting opensocial.group spec thoughts / questions I added to a Tangled issue: Unfortunately Tangled doesn’t let me subscribe to the repo and get email notifications so it seems worth posting over here too. Tangled Basic metadata for modality spaces. #15 Me @lou.gg and @erlend.sh were discussing interoperability between different apps around the idea of "threads" in the context of things like forum threads and chat threads. The thought right now is that forum threads and chat threads are clearly... Me @lou.gg and @erlend.sh were discussing interoperability between different apps around the idea of “threads” in the context of things like forum threads and chat threads. The thought right now is that forum threads and chat threads are clearly different modalities that might want different handling, so they should have their own lexicons. Still, I do think there’s value in having all of these threads be able to describe themselves in a somewhat universal way. Almost like OG metadata for permissioned spaces. There are a few different sides of this that I think might be useful to have standardized in opensocial.group and wanted to get feedback. Standardized Metadata Records for Spaces My thought is that we can create something like a group.opensocial.space.meta/self record in every space that has some minimal metadata that can be used to inform other apps what the space is about even if it can’t directly interact with the modality because it isn’t supported. For example some basics like title, description, image / avatar, or feature image would allow us to make something like a link preview for a space in any app regardless of modality. The current proposal already has records in the members/self space that has a title and description for a space, but I think that it’d probably be best if there was metadata in the space, so that any space that you get an at:// URI and a credential to can also be described just by looking at its meta record. Announcing a Space Publicly Another use-case that we had was the ability to index threads across the atmosphere. We already have a declaration record in this spec for announcing the existence of a group on the firehose, and I think it could be useful to have a standard for doing the same thing for spaces. This would make it possible, for example, to have an AppView that indexes all of the public forum topics created across any group, possibly filtering based on the space’s modality. Cross-posting opensocial.group spec thoughts / questions I added to a Tangled issue:

 Unfortunately Tangled doesn’t let me subscribe to the repo and get email notifications so it seems worth posting over here too.

 Tangled 

 Basic metadata for modality spaces. #15 

 Me @lou.gg and @erlend.sh were discussing interoperability between different apps around the idea of "threads" in the context of things like forum threads and chat threads. The thought right now is that forum threads and chat threads are clearly...

 Me @lou.gg and @erlend.sh were discussing interoperability between different apps around the idea of “threads” in the context of things like forum threads and chat threads. The thought right now is that forum threads and chat threads are clearly different modalities that might want different handling, so they should have their own lexicons. Still, I do think there’s value in having all of these threads be able to describe themselves in a somewhat universal way. Almost like OG metadata for permissioned spaces.

 There are a few different sides of this that I think might be useful to have standardized in opensocial.group and wanted to get feedback.

 Standardized Metadata Records for Spaces

 My thought is that we can create something like a group.opensocial.space.meta/self record in every space that has some minimal metadata that can be used to inform other apps what the space is about even if it can’t directly interact with the modality because it isn’t supported. For example some basics like title, description, image / avatar, or feature image would allow us to make something like a link preview for a space in any app regardless of modality.

 The current proposal already has records in the members/self space that has a title and description for a space, but I think that it’d probably be best if there was metadata in the space, so that any space that you get an at:// URI and a credential to can also be described just by looking at its meta record.

 Announcing a Space Publicly

 Another use-case that we had was the ability to index threads across the atmosphere. We already have a declaration record in this spec for announcing the existence of a group on the firehose, and I think it could be useful to have a standard for doing the same thing for spaces.

 This would make it possible, for example, to have an AppView that indexes all of the public forum topics created across any group, possibly filtering based on the space’s modality.

 I’m imagining that a space declaration record would contain simply the space’s at:// URI, and AppViews could ignore that contain URIs with space types that they are not interested in.

 Providing a Default App for Space Links?

 This is a little more uncertain, but it occurs to me that it would be useful to be able to, for example, post something that resolves to an at:// link to an AtmoBB forum topic in a Roomy chat message, and have Roomy be able to display an inline link to the forum topic with the title automatically fetched from the metadata record.

 I’m imagining, at the underlying data level, when that chat message gets stored on protocol, it would be best if that link could come with an at:// URI to the space that is being linked to. That would allow, for example, certain apps that support the AtmoBB lexicon to open the forum topic without leaving the app, instead of it being just a link to the AtmoBB app.

 But if the app doesn’t support AtmoBB’s lexicon, then it would like to link to some app that can display the forum topic properly. Maybe it would make sense for the space metadata record to also contain a link that can be used to view the thread in the app that created it? That way, given just an at:// URI to a space, any app can display the basic information for the space, and know which link to send the user to if they would like to view it in its native app.

 Note: how to get the at:// URI when a user pastes in a link to a specific app is a separate, but related concern which looks like it has been discussed here on the forum.

These are interesting, thanks for sharing!

 Standardized Metadata Records for Spaces

 From the opensocial.group perspective, it feels nice to be able to enumerate this kind of metadata without needing to synchronize/fetch a metadata record from each individual space. Especially for space types (modalities) which the displaying app might not have permission to synchronize (aka, might not have OAuth scopes to synchronize spaces of a given type).

 From the perspective of public spaces and wanting to do cross-app preview cards, that feels like a generic thing that all spaces might want to support, not just opensocial.group spaces. Maybe a community.lexicon.* description record would make sense?

 Announcing a Space Publicly

 I think there is something to this. I’m not sure if opensocial.group is the right abstraction layer to handle it though. On the one hand it might be a generic need for all public spaces, not just opensocial.group spaces, and a more generic declaration might be good. On the other hand it can also be helpful in the public broadcast protocol to have distinct record types for different modalities (eg, to help backfill using listReposByCollection ).

 I almost feel like using the space modality as a record “collection” (NSID) might make sense (with the record key matching the space key), but that is probably too clever/confusing.

 Providing a Default App for Space Links?

 A bit of a broken record, but this also feels like a more generic issue than opensocial.group, or even spaces. My general take on this is that is a problem for the displaying app to solve, using the record type and/or space type in the URI. It makes sense to have some fallback mechanism to hint to apps how to construct an app URL for content types they don’t know about, but it feels like that could be as simple as a collectively-maintained JSON file in a git repo somewhere, or some way for lexicon developers to declare default URL patterns by publishing a record.

bnewbold.net: 

 feels like a generic thing that all spaces might want to support, not just opensocial.group spaces

 Yeah, good point. In my head I was subconsciously batching it all into opensocial.group since it was the first “generic” standard on top of ATProto spaces. But I think you’re right that all these points are basically universal, regardless of the group host standard for the most part.

 bnewbold.net: 

 From the opensocial.group perspective, it feels nice to be able to enumerate this kind of metadata without needing to synchronize/fetch a metadata record from each individual space. Especially for space types (modalities) which the displaying app might not have permission to synchronize (aka, might not have OAuth scopes to synchronize spaces of a given type).

 Oh, I didn’t think about the oauth scope to synchronize different types of spaces. That’s a little annoying for the general-purpose link-card type use-case.

 And it’s also problematic in many cases to have access to the space’s metadata be separate from the space’s own access. I’m imagining title’s like “What are we going to do about @some-user ’s behavior on the forum?” in a private space for moderator chats, and that not being appropriate to show to the whole group.

 It does make me think that maybe for the link-sharing use-case that the link metadata should be wrapped up in the chat message when someone sends it, so you’re essentially re-posting to the metadata to the app, instead of expecting the app having to get it from the space.

 That has the same metadata leakage problem, but the app can be clear about that in the chat preview that it’s showing the title ( and let you remove it and just paste the bare link ).

 bnewbold.net: 

 On the other hand it can also be helpful in the public broadcast protocol to have distinct record types for different modalities (eg, to help backfill using listReposByCollection ).

 I almost feel like using the space modality as a record “collection” (NSID) might make sense (with the record key matching the space key), but that is probably too clever/confusing.

 I know. The case is even stronger for doing something a little too clever now that I think about listReposByCollection , which hadn’t occurred to me yet. Also relevant is jetstream filtering.

 Honestly doing a weird sub-domaining to the collection where the declaration record for a space.roomy.channel would be, for example, community.lexicon.space.declaration.space.roomy.channel/tid might actually be a good solution. I think you don’t need to worry about the tid matching the space key since you still need to put the full at:// URI in a record field anyway.

 I know you’re not supposed to “generate” collection IDs, but in this case it does map one-to-one to an actual space type lexicon.

So, continuing to think about this, focusing on space metadata: what would people think about using standard.site to describe things like forum threads?

 @schlage.town @awarm.space , trying to find standard.site people to ask about this because it’s actually something that was somewhat unclear to me about standard.site: what is the scope of standard.site do you think? Should we not use it for things like forum topics or chat threads?

 It’s super generic and provides basic metadata that is pretty universal, but should it stay used for pretty blog-like data?

 Group stuff is still obviously nascent, but are there people interested in adopting a universal “thread” lexicon similar, at least in principle, to standard.site?

Hey yeah good question! Personally I think it’s better for standard.site to stay focused on longform blog-like content. Not that it has to be strictly blogging only, I think it’s a bit fuzzy and that’s fine, but yes I’d say something like forum threads should be a different lexicon!

 This has come up before b/c it’s not super well defined and there are definitely cases where folks want to use it even where (imo) it doesn’t always make sense. In a reply a while back to a similar q in signal I said:

 Yeah, imo a bit broader than blogs but definitely narrower than any content on the internet haha.

 Easier to think in terms of why you’d want to publish as standard.site, so less about ‘could the data technically fit into these lexicons’, more about: does it fit the use case of social reading and publishing ?

 Would readers want to find this content in discovery tools? Would I want to see if my mutuals are publishing this kind of thing?

 So, things like web comics, serialized novels, journalism, project newsletters — yes! Status logs, patent records — I think no. Of course some ambiguity / grey area but maybe that’s a helpful way to think about it?

 Reasonable for folks to disagree on exactly where the line should be but just for me at least I don’t think I’d want to see forum / chat threads e.g. in a reader app or discovery tool, though I’d be into a similar thing more for that purpose!

value.title: Two things I'd change in the spec, and one record I'd like to add
value.description: I put a version of this in Brett’s thread back in Sept and showed the running demo on Bluesky a week later, so here’s the general form. Context: I’ve been building payments for atproto apps out of Europe since the summer - it’s called atmopay . I didn’t build it on this spec, and I’d rather say that than have someone notice. Different records, kept in different places, different way of asking whether someone’s paid. But it would be very good to have a shared standard, so here are some suggestions up for discussion: 1. The servicer list shouldn’t sit in the DID document The docs are already of two minds as far as I can tell. Recipients says publish an ordered list of broker DIDs in your DID document. App Developers says “it is up to the recipient to contextually hint or broadcast which payment servicers they use.” So it’s half-settled already, and I’d suggest to settle it as a record. The reason: that list is the creator’s off switch. Take a broker off it and every app on the network stops believing their attestations, and you don’t need the broker’s cooperation to do it. Best property in the design as far as I can tell. And right now it lives behind the most nerve-wracking write in atproto (DID op) With more than one broker around it matters even more. In atmopay ’s spec authorizedIssuers lets an app find out which ones a creator uses. 2. payment.lookup needs a lock on it Required payer and recipient, no auth declared, and the broker guide leaves authentication to each broker. For sure, some will take the easy path. Then it’s a who-paid-whom endpoint for the whole network, which undoes most of what the permissioned-space mode is there for. Not a free change, I know. Every scenario verifies through lookup. But App Developers already documents local verification straight from the payer’s repo, and that path never touches it. So a lock doesn’t stop you verifying a payment you’ve been pointed at but rather stops you discovering the ones nobody told you about. In atmopay the endpoint answers two callers: the subject, or a service the creator has named. Everyone else gets the same refusal whether or not the account exists, so the error doesn’t leak either. The record I’d like to add Scope says catalogues, pricing and tiers are out. That’s fair, but it’s the first wall an app hits: no checkout screen without knowing what’s for sale. That’s the piece I’d most like to see land somewhere shared. I don’t much mind where. Paying the app that delivered it. In atmopay the delivering app as well as the selling one get a share of the transaction fees. Delivery is attested by the reader’s own PDS, because the space access check names the client, and the selling app signs with its own PDS. What’s missing is that service auth names the user and never the app. I have a short write-up on that. Spec, lexicons, a verifier, a mock issuer and the pilot ( pnpm start , nothing external) for what atmopay uses can be found here: https://github.com/eurosky-social/atproto-paym

value.title: Common "langs" type?
value.description: I am wondering if there is a lexicon type out there intended for folks to use in their own lexicons for i18n. Bluesky has their langs field. Others could emulate it, but there’s not much momentum or incentive to do so. If there were a well made internationalization type that I could use in my lexicons, it would be a lot easier for me to adopt that and for i18n behavior to be more consistent across lexicons. For example, in this lex I have a langs field modeled after Bluesky’s approach. { "lexicon": 1, "id": "community.lexicon.rating.prompt", "description": "A prompt or question that a rating answers, clarifying what aspect of a subject is being evaluated.", "defs": { "main": { "type": "record", "key": "tid", "record": { "type": "object", "required": ["text"], "properties": { "text": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 1024, "description": "The prompt or question text." }, "langs": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string", "format": "language" }, "maxItems": 3, "description": "BCP-47 tag(s) the prompt text is written in." }, "createdAt": { "type": "string", "format": "datetime" } } } } } } But instead what if it just borrowed an existing type for language tagging. { "lexicon": 1, "id": "community.lexicon.rating.prompt", "description": "A prompt or question that a rating answers, clarifying what aspect of a subject is being evaluated.", "defs": { "main": { "type": "record", "key": "tid", "record": { "type": "object", "required": ["text"], "properties": { "text": { "type": "string", "maxLength": 1024, "description": "The prompt or question text." }, "langs": { "type": "ref", "ref": "some.i18n.thing", }, "createdAt": { "type": "string", "format": "datetime" } } } } } } Thoughts? If I missed an existing topic on this my apologies.

value.textContent:
Ahh, a way to offer translations of a given on-protocol string inside the record?

 I know Scan/PaddingLabs was looking at building a translations app/lexicon, which would need a lexicon that represents translations, but they’d probably each have their own record.

 I figure this would be a structure specifically for multi-lingual people, who want to be able to store different localisations of the same text on a supporting record. It seems fairly edge-case to me, though I’ve used the Bluesky pattern you mention in some lexicons.

 I’ll take a look through my lexicon estate and see where something like this might be useful!

Not even necessarily translations, but language tagging records so that they can be marked appropriately. Showing relevant content to people of different primary languages. Does also help for queuing browser and device translation.

My guess is that having the convention of it being a top-level field named langs and having array-of-strings type is more important for reuse than having a declared lexicon schema to reference. For such a simple thing having a layer of indirection doesn’t feel worth it: easier for humans and machines to understand the lexicon-in-place than needing to go resolve the reference.

 Generic app frameworks (like HappyView) could look for that data pattern, either in raw data or looking at the Lexicon schema.

 (just my 2c)

Just as a side note, there have been some issues filed for Bluesky because it uses (as far as I understood) ISO 639-1 with incomplete ISO 639-2 fallback.

 I too prefer BCP 47 anyway though, since that’s vastly easier to use on the web and has better coverage. Its registry also looks very good to me in terms of being easy to process, for friendly naming in English UIs.

I think end users might be somewhat familiar with it too (or at least may recognise their own language and region tags) since they appear in URLs of localised sites quite often.

hi!

 I’ve a languages field in lichen wiki lexicon, I’m using BCP 47.

 Felt like it was the best fit for lexicons as well.

We talked about this topic in the BlamPow Discord a bit (though this isn’t a summary of that discussion, just my own two cents for the most part after being made aware of the issue):

 It would be great to be able to explicitly indicate prominent language-agnostic or no-language content while localised content may also be present in the same presentation unit.

 For example, if someone writes a post “Wow, endlich fertig!” and attaches a photo of their painting, or writes “So süß!” and a photo of a sleeping kitten, that crosses language borders quite easily, and most recipients hopefully wouldn’t care too much if they can’t read the caption right away. (That means calligraphy and graffiti may also be considered prominently language-agnostic if the author intends them to be, even if they consist of text carrying language.)

 It would be helpful to reduce or ignore language filters in discovery in such cases. I’m aware this is tricky to do in general (so as not to create a “ ”-button for reach that every spammer would press), but for example Feeds could indicate that they require weaker filters .

I’m thinking of e.g. For You or Popular with Friends -style Feeds, which already strongly filter by user group or proximity, respectively, or Mutuals (which in my opinion shouldn’t be language-filtered at all by default). A Feed like Hot Links on the other hand looks like it would want to at least default to strict language filters across the board.

 Semi-relatedly: From a user perspective, I’d really like to be able to adjust the filter on the fly more easily. It would be great if that was unobtrusively surfaced in e.g. the Home/Feed view header(s) in Bluesky-compatible apps.

value.title: A general purpose ratings lexicon
value.description: I took a stab at solving ratings for everyone forever. I’d love your thoughts. tynanistyping.offprint.app Rating all the things | Tynan Purdy ⁂ | Offprint All existing proposals are wrong because they are all right
value.textContent:
I took a stab at solving ratings for everyone forever. I’d love your thoughts.

 tynanistyping.offprint.app 

 Rating all the things | Tynan Purdy ⁂ | Offprint 

 All existing proposals are wrong because they are all right

This seems solid; it’s definitely powerful enough to support most rating systems.

 However, I’m working with rating systems in games, like Chess’ Elo ratings. It’s arguably a distinct space, but this lexicon is VERY close to encompassing it already.

 However, the rating subject union only includes URIs and strongRefs, but not DIDs. While my rating service could point at some profile record, the semantics of rating the player directly seems cleaner.

 Additionally, we might want to know a given player’s rating over time. A service might want to dump a set of historical ratings on the protocol. My thought is that we need a field to allow identities to express WHEN the rating was given in cases where that doesn’t match createdAt. Perhaps “ratedAt”? I’d think we’d want it optional, since createdAt can stand in for it in the more common case where those values should match.

Thanks! I admit there is some ambiguity because words collide in meaning. Something like ELO rating would fall under an aggregation or analysis, rather than an individual instance of rating something. ELO is computed on your wins and losses. Writing a record would be like saying “I say your elo is 4”, which doesn’t mean much. The rating record is a statement of opinion in response to a prompt and subject. ELO and other stats are business logic.

 On the note of subject including DIDs, good point! I was hesitant to include it at first due to the ickyness of rating an account as a whole (the facebook flashbacks ) but I agree it does have utility.

 For backdating, I believe you can edit the createdAt to indicate when the record is from. A lot of social archive importers do this (hence some atproto accounts have records from before 2022). I brought in my old Instagram posts and they are dated accurately.

Indeed, Elo is computed on wins/losses. But by whom? With what inputs? People and organizations might differ on disqualifications and game results.

 Modern chess ratings are the FIDE org answering the prompt “how good is {subject}” at {blitz|rapid|classical} chess" by publishing two new ratings after every game. The Elo system itself maps nicely to a scale. It’s a rating, and your proposal solves ratings forever (as long as it allows DID subjects).

 But… yeah. Systems where people rate others could easily be creepy or harmful. Let’s discourage and criticize such things but not limit our language by excluding the category. The original Facebook should be socially unacceptable, not technically impossible.

 And I see, createdAt can serve. We would be dropping the import time info, but I suppose it doesn’t matter.

There being multiple potential answers to ‘computed by whom on what?’ is exactly the point. putting the raw data on protocol allows for a marketplace of services on top of that information. Trust signals and service quality are differentiators. If you wanted to document an ELO at a particular time I don’t see why the current lex set would prevent that. If you wanted to also offer some proof of what went into that calculation, I think that would be left to a sidecar record.

 I’ll add DID as an option for the subject.

Agreed. I think this lexicon fits well for recording the results of such rating calculations. This would naturally be in addition to publishing the underlying game records the ratings are computed from. The raw data belongs on the protocol, as do the outputs of the marketplace of services built atop it.

 Thanks, I’ll look forward to publishing my game’s ratings this way!

 PS: just put some thought into the sidecar pattern here: it’s good, with one caveat. If you model a parent-child, N-1 relationship, make sure to prevent the invalid N-N cases structurally. Logic that prevents a second sidecar from being written can work, but defining the sidecar rkey as the child record’s tid or URI makes the invalid states unrepresentable.

Hey everyone!

 We haven’t pushed out any breaking changes the last couple weeks but we did land some this week, specifically centered around the simplespace API.

 Two main pieces of work landed:

 Matthieu’s review & cleanup of the implementation: Permissioned data review by matthieusieben · Pull Request #5469 · bluesky-social/atproto · GitHub 

 An update that makes simplespace write access (storing & forwarding a write notification) independent of read access (getting a space credential): Add independent write access to simplespaces by dholms · Pull Request #5496 · bluesky-social/atproto · GitHub 

 The relevant change to the proposal is over here: 0016 Atproto spaces: simplespace write access by dholms · Pull Request #105 · bluesky-social/proposals · GitHub 

 This change is necessary to support the currently proposed “invites” spaces in the atmosphere groups standard: Thoughts on atmosphere groups "Invite" space 

 Here’s a description of relevant breaking changes:

 simplespace lexicons

 policy split into required readPolicy/writePolicy

 addMember replaced by putMember

 read & write booleans on members

 @atproto /car

 CAR SDK moved from @atproto /common into a new @atproto /car

 some updated reader/lifecycle APIs

 @atproto /space

 Some type tightening & renaming

 @atproto /syntax

 removed atUri.spaceRef() in favor of SpaceRef.for() 

 We deployed the spaces alpha PDS, published an updated docker image at ghcr.io/bluesky-social/atproto:pds-spaces-alpha , and published new alpha snapshot packages on NPM for all relevant packages.

 This does involve a database migration on the PDS. To reduce the operational burden for folks that are running a self-hosted PDS, I opted to make that something that runs the first time each user’s actor DB is opened ( relevant commit ) for now. This approach will likely change before the production distribution.

Heads up, we’ll be doing another release this Thurs (Oct 1)!

 It will likely include the following changes:

 shorten space credential expiration & add revocation method 

 switch out DPoP for HTTP Signatures 

 add sequencing to space host for more reliable space sync 

 We are currently going back over the repo serialization & commit format. This will not be a part of the release this week, but will likely be done next week or the week after.

value.description: I’m working through the technical details and want to confirm my understanding. Currently it is not possible for a feed server to independently verify the membership of an identity to a space with formal protocol channels or mechanics. did:plc:foo authenticates with ExampleApp https://example.app/ ExampleApp creates service-auth token for getFeedSkeleton on behalf of did:plc:foo to FeedServer https://feeds.app/ ExampleApp requests getFeedSkeleton from FeedServer https://feeds.app/ for did:plc:foo with the service-auth token FeedServer has no ability to determine if did:plc:foo is a member of space did:plc:bar/com.example.space/baz For FeedServer to know if did:plc:foo is a member of space did:plc:bar/com.example.space/baz, one of these must happen: The feed server has its own auth where it gets an identity access token and can mint a space credential to test authentication. This sucks for a lot of reasons. The AppView sends additional data* that must be trusted that says the requesting identity has access to the space. This sucks for different reasons. The space must be configured with a membership-app that can be queried by FeedServer directly. This sucks also sucks for different reasons. I propose that the checkUserAccess be implemented by the space host and can be queried with service authentication by members of the space. That would allow FeedServer to install a “service account” as a member of the space that could then make service auth requests as needed.

I’m working through the technical details and want to confirm my understanding.

 Currently it is not possible for a feed server to independently verify the membership of an identity to a space with formal protocol channels or mechanics.

 did:plc:foo authenticates with ExampleApp https://example.app/ 

 ExampleApp creates service-auth token for getFeedSkeleton on behalf of did:plc:foo to FeedServer https://feeds.app/ 

 ExampleApp requests getFeedSkeleton from FeedServer https://feeds.app/ for did:plc:foo with the service-auth token

 FeedServer has no ability to determine if did:plc:foo is a member of space did:plc:bar/com.example.space/baz

 For FeedServer to know if did:plc:foo is a member of space did:plc:bar/com.example.space/baz, one of these must happen:

 The feed server has its own auth where it gets an identity access token and can mint a space credential to test authentication. This sucks for a lot of reasons.

 The AppView sends additional data* that must be trusted that says the requesting identity has access to the space. This sucks for different reasons.

 The space must be configured with a membership-app that can be queried by FeedServer directly. This sucks also sucks for different reasons.

 I propose that the checkUserAccess be implemented by the space host and can be queried with service authentication by members of the space. That would allow FeedServer to install a “service account” as a member of the space that could then make service auth requests as needed.
